cognate: Agent noun *déh₃tor- 'giver' (Ved. dātár-, Av. dātar-, Gk δωτήρ/δώτωρ) governing the genitive plural of *h₁wesu- 'good (things)': Ved. vásūnām, Av. vohunąm, Gk ἑάων. Gk ἑάων occurs in Homer only in δωτῆρες/δῶτορ ἑάων and in Il. 24.528, where the same genitive plural depends on δίδωσι 'gives' (Zeus's jar of goods), i.e. the verbal correspondent of the agent-noun phrase.
drift_or_renewal: In the packet Vedic lines the genitive object is renewed: rāyáḥ ... dātā́ (RV 6.23.10d, rayí- 'wealth' for vásu-) and figura etymologica dātrásya dātā́ 'giver of the gift' (RV 9.97.55c); the old vásūnām survives in RV 8.51.5a and in Avestan vohunąm dātārō. In Il. 24.528 the agent noun is replaced by the finite verb δίδωσι, a natural verbal transform of 'giver of goods'.
shared_syntax: agent noun in -tor- + objective genitive plural of 'good(s)'; predicated of a god or gods
context: All are divine epithets for the gods as dispensers of good things: Indra and Soma/Bhaga in the RV lines, Ahura Mazda and the Aməša Spəṇtas in Avestan, the gods (θεοί) and Hermes in Homer/Hesiod, Zeus allotting goods from his jars in Il. 24.528. The Greek phrase preserves an archaism (ἑάων, a word otherwise dead in Homer) that only makes sense as an inherited formula.
phrase: *déh₃tores h₁wesuHom 'givers of good things' (pie-root deh₃- + *h₁wésu-), predicated of the gods

support.locus: KUB 27.1 Rs. III 11; KUB 11.31 Vs. I 4; KBo 3.16+ Rev. III 7′ (and ~14 more)

words.etymon: *dʰeh₁- 'put' (packet mapping to 'give' is wrong: Hitt. dai- 'put' < *dʰeh₁-)

cognate: Hitt. kiššari / kišri (loc. sg.) is the exact match of Gk χειρί (dat.-loc., *ǵʰesr-í); Ved. háste is the same root with a -to- stem. The verb is *dʰeh₁- in all three: Hitt. dai-, Gk τίθημι, Ved. dhā-.
drift_or_renewal: Packet AVP 19.9.18 has antar hastam kṛtaṃ 'placed/made within my hand' (kṛ- for dhā-; cf. the AV dice formula kṛtaṃ me dakṣiṇe haste), the Ṛgveda keeps háste dhā-. Hittite has the verb pai- 'give' in the variant kišri pianzi; 'right' is written logographically (ZAG-ni) and cannot be compared lexically.
shared_syntax: locative of 'hand' + 'put' with the object handed over (into someone's (right) hand)
context: Ritual/ceremonial handing over: in Hittite festival texts the priest puts cedar or bread into the king's (right) hand; in Homer cups, prizes and gifts are put 'into the hands' of a recipient at feast and games; in the RV a god places the vajra or goods in his right hand. Hittite and Vedic share the specification 'right hand'.

support.locus: Alvíssmál 16 (edda:7094, labelled Volundarkviða 16 by the loader)

cognate: Sun-word *sóh₂wl̥ / *sh₂uén- (Lat. sōl, Ved. sū́rya-/svàr-, Gk ἥλιος, ON sól) + a wheel-word. Lat. rota and Ved. rátha- are the same formation *Hrot-h₂- (Lith. ratas, OIr. roth, OHG rad 'wheel'); Ved. cakrá-, Gk κύκλος, ON hvél are exact cognates *kʷékʷlo-.
drift_or_renewal: *Hrot-h₂- kept the old sense 'wheel' in Latin (sōlis rota) but shifted to 'chariot' in Indo-Iranian, so Ved. sū́ryasya rátha- 'the Sun's chariot' is the drifted form of the same collocation, while the 'wheel' slot is filled in Vedic by the synonym cakrá- (sū́ryasya cakrám; the sun's one-wheeled chariot ratham eka cakram in AVŚ 9.9.3). Greek and Norse use the *kʷékʷlo- word. Caveat: Lucretius is strongly Hellenizing and Greek ἡλίου κύκλος is attested only in tragedy, so solis rota could be modelled on Greek; the claim survives because the image is carried independently by Vedic (sū́ryasya cakrám, RV) and Norse (Alvíssmál fagrahvél) with the inherited *kʷékʷlo- word, and Latin rota itself is the inherited *Hrot-h₂- word. AVŚ 9.9.3 (= RV 1.164 riddle) does not name the sun; its one-wheeled chariot is the sun only by the standard interpretation.
shared_syntax: genitive of 'sun' + head noun 'wheel' (or 'chariot'); the sun's wheel as subject/object of motion
context: Cosmological descriptions of the sun's course: Lucretius on the size and motion of the solar disc ('solis rota'), the Atharvaveda on the Sun's horses drawing his chariot and the seven yoking the one-wheeled chariot. Same image of the sun as a wheel/wheeled vehicle.
phrase: *séh₂wl̥-os Hrot-h₂- / *kʷékʷlo- 'the wheel of the sun' (with Indo-Iranian drift to 'the sun's chariot')

cognate: *h₂éwsōs 'Dawn' (Ved. uṣás-, Gk ἠώς) with the verb *bʰeh₂- 'shine, appear' (Ved. bhā-, vi-bhā-; Gk φαίνομαι, aor. φάνη) and its nominal derivative (Ved. bhānú- 'radiance', Gk φάος 'light'), plus an epithet from *dyew- 'heaven' (Ved. devī́ 'goddess', Gk δῖα 'heavenly').
drift_or_renewal: Gk φαίνω is a -yé- present (*bʰh₂-n-yé-) where Vedic has the root present bhāti; Gk φάος (*bʰéh₂-wos) vs Ved. bhānú- (*bʰeh₂-nu-) differ in suffix only. The epithets are parallel derivatives rather than one form: Ved. devī́ (*deyw-ih₂) vs Gk δῖα (*diw-yeh₂, = Ved. divyá-).
shared_syntax: subject Dawn + intransitive 'shines forth/appears', very often as a participle used as a time phrase (Ved. uṣásaḥ vibhātī́ḥ, Gk ἅμ' ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι); genitive construction 'the light/radiance of Dawn' (uṣásaḥ bhānúḥ ~ φάος Ἠοῦς); Dawn qualified as 'heavenly/goddess' (devī́m uṣásam vibhātī́m ~ φανήμεναι Ἠῶ δῖαν, ἠὼς ὅτε δῖα φανήῃ)
context: In both traditions this is the stock way of marking daybreak, with the deified Dawn as subject: RV hymns to Uṣas (3.61, 7.78) and the Homeric dawn formulas that open episodes (Il. 1.477, Od. 13.94 the morning star announcing the light of Dawn). In both corpora the collocation is formulaic: about 20 RV pādas join uṣás- with bhā-, about 40 Homeric lines join ἠώς with φαίνω, and the epithet *dyew-derivative + 'shine' recurs (RV 3.61.2a úṣo devi ... ví bhāhi ~ Il. 9.240 φανήμεναι Ἠῶ δῖαν).
phrase: *h₂éwsōs (diwyeh₂) bʰeh₂- 'heavenly Dawn shines forth'; participle *h₂ewsōs bʰeh₂-nt- as a time formula; *bʰeh₂-wos/-nu- h₂ewsos 'light of Dawn'

words.etymon: *deywós 'god' (+ dēls, not cognate with Ved. nápāt or Gk κοῦρος)
*h₂éwsōs + *h₂wes- 'shine at dawn' (context: ā́yukṣātām aśvínā yā́tave rátham)

cognate: The genitive of the sky-god (*diw-és > Ved. diváḥ, Gk Διός) or his derivative *deywós (Latv. Dievs) + a kinship noun designating divine children: Ved. diváḥ nápātā (the Aśvins), diváḥ duhitā́ (Uṣas); Gk Διὸς κοῦροι; Latv. Dieva dēli. Ved. duhitár- matches Gk θυγάτηρ and Lith. duktė only outside this packet.
drift_or_renewal: Kinship noun renewed in each branch (Ved. nápāt-, Gk κοῦρος, Latv. dēls); in Baltic the genitive is from *deywós 'god', the appellative derived from *dyew-, rather than the sky-name itself. The 'sky's daughter' role passes in Baltic to Saules meita 'Sun's daughter' (cf. Ved. duhitā́ sū́ryasya).
shared_syntax: genitive of the sky god + noun for 'son(s)/daughter' as a fixed title
context: Mythologically congruent: the divine twins are horsemen who appear at dawn. RV 1.157.1 opens with Dawn shining forth and the Aśvins yoking their chariot to drive; in the Latvian song the singer climbs to heaven and finds 'the son of God saddling his horse' and greets him 'good morning' (Labrītiņ); BV 34017 pairs the Dieva dēli with the Sun's daughter, as the Aśvins are paired with Sūryā. Dawn as diváḥ duhitā́ (RV 1.92.5d) belongs to the same family of titles. Note: RV 1.157.1b matches through its context line (ā́yukṣātām aśvínā yā́tave rátham), not through the passage line itself.
phrase: *diwós + kinship noun (renewed in each branch: Ved. nápāt-, Gk κοῦρος, Latv. dēls; Lith. Dievo sūneliai, recalled, would give *suHnú-) 'sons of Sky', beside *diwós dʰugh₂tḗr 'daughter of Sky': the horse-riding Divine Twins at dawn

cognate: Both members are cognate: Lat. diēs ~ Ved. dívā (instr. 'by day', *diw-éh₁), Lat. nox/noctēs ~ Ved. nákt-/náktam (*nókʷt-).
drift_or_renewal: Latin diēs is a new nominal stem from the accusative *dyēm, used adverbially in the plural ('days and nights' = 'all the time'); Vedic keeps adverbial case forms (dívā, náktam). Greek renews 'day' (νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ). The packet's Vedic passage only has the related dual dvandva uṣā́sā-náktā 'Dawn and Night' in its context, so the Vedic merism itself comes from support.
shared_syntax: coordinated 'day' + 'night' as a temporal merism meaning 'always, continuously'
context: Plautus: someone spends 'days and nights' hunting (Cas. 320), the things not bought with money listed as 'day, water, sun, moon, night' (As. 198). In the RV dívā náktam 'by day and by night' asks for unceasing protection. Both use the pair for totality of time.
